sources.title: Looksmaxxing may point to deeper body image issues in young men, mental health expert says
Looksmaxxing isn't just a TikTok trend, it often reflects severe body image issues in boys and young men
'Looksmaxxing' is all over TikTok. Our experts take a closer look.
A look into extreme beauty trend 'looksmaxxing' gaining popularity in young men (video, NBC News)

chunks.text: A new word has {{caught on}} online [[among]] teenage boys and young men. Looksmaxxing means improving your [[appearance]] as much as possible. The soft version is [[grooming]] and a [[daily routine]] of sleep and exercise. The hard version is [[surgery]] on the nose or the [[jawline]]. Many who follow it are still {{growing up}}, and they {{look up to}} influencers who give a face a [[rating]] [[out of ten]].

chunks.text: A social worker at the University of Michigan wrote in July 2026 that these behaviors look like the [[signs]] of an [[eating disorder]] or [[body dysmorphia]]. Some young men {{cut out}} [[whole food groups]] or {{give up}} meals for days. A few hit their own face with a [[hammer]]. She says the [[trend]] is not [[harmless]], and that a boy who starts small can {{end up}} in danger.

chunks.text: Looksmaxxing spreads because it pays to {{show off}}. A researcher at Northeastern University says the most [[extreme]] [[stunts]] get the most clicks, so the advice keeps getting harder. He also says the [[ideal]] face in these videos copies old European [[beauty standards]]. A [[psychologist]] there says men are a new market for beauty companies. For some boys it stops being a hobby and can {{take over}} the whole day, and the wish to {{stand out}} turns into a fear of being [[judged]].

chunks.text: Doctors {{point out}} that the problem is easy to [[miss]] in boys. Most tests ask about a fear of being fat, so a boy who trains hard to look [[lean]] can pass them. Researchers estimate that [[one in three]] people with an eating disorder is male. The [[warning signs]] include [[obsessive]] mirror checks and secret rules about food. Experts say it is healthy to {{work out}}, but they advise parents to help a son {{open up}} and to [[seek help]] early, because [[self-esteem]] problems can have [[long-term]] effects.
